By Beth Nichols

Overview

The compact Nissan Rogue won’t excite you, but it can cosset you with its comfy seats, a smooth ride, and leave-it-to-me driver aids. The Platinum model—swathed in quilted leather upholstery and equipped with hands-free-capable adaptive cruise control—is nice enough inside to make you think "luxury crossover."

As for how the Rogue drives? It’s easygoing. Unhurried. Undistinguished. Its standard turbocharged three-cylinder engine makes a respectable 201 horsepower and is a touch easier on fuel than its competition, according to the EPA. It does its job quietly, driving the front or all four wheels without fuss through a gearless continuously variable transmission. This is a brutally competitive class, though, and the Rogue—decent as it is—is outshone by more than a dozen other SUVs in our ratings.

Expert Tip: Consider taking a Honda CR-V, Mazda CX-50, or Volkswagen Tiguan for a spin before signing papers for the Rogue.

What's New for 2026?

A Dark Armor trim joins the Rogue lineup for 2026. It’s essentially a black-heavy SV trim with a 360-degree camera system, a panoramic sunroof, and heating for the front seats and steering wheel.

C/D Expert Tip:

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

Pricing and Which One to Buy

The SV trim offers a reasonable amount of standard features for the money. It improves on the no-frills base model with proximity keyless entry and push-button start, dual-zone automatic climate control, remote start, and several driver-assistance features. Heated front seats and a heated steering wheel are available, too.

Compare Cars

Engine, Transmission, and Performance

  • Engine: 201-hp turbocharged 1.5-liter three-cylinder
  • Transmission: continuously variable automatic (CVT)
  • Drivetrains: front-wheel drive, all-wheel drive

Front-wheel drive is standard on all but the ostensibly rugged Rock Creek model, which comes exclusively with all-wheel drive. This latter drivetrain is available throughout the lineup, however, for an extra cost. On the road, the Rogue delivers a compliant ride that's agreeable for commuting and road-tripping, but it's not the least engaging or fun on a winding road, which is why its blasé driving demeanor hasn't earned it any fans among our staff.

Don’t think the Rogue Rock Creek can hang with the Ford Bronco Sport on an off-road trail, either. While the Rock Creek sets itself apart from other trims with trail-oriented visual touches, hill-descent control, and all-terrain tires, it lacks underbody protection and rides at the same height as other Rogues. It’ll tackle dirt roads with ease, but nothing extreme.

0–60-MPH Times

  • C/D 60-mph Test: 8.0 seconds (Platinum AWD)

In Comparison: In our testing, the Rogue's 60-mph time is only a 0.2-second improvement over its naturally aspirated predecessor’s time, but the turbocharged three-cylinder in this generation makes the Rogue feel perkier than before.

Towing and Payload Capacity

The Rogue can tow up to 1500 pounds when properly equipped.

Fuel Economy and Real-World MPG

  • C/D 75-mph Highway Fuel-Economy Test: 31 mpg (Platinum AWD)
  • EPA City Ratings: 27-29 mpg
  • EPA Highway Ratings: 32-36 mpg

With the turbocharged three-cylinder engine onboard, the Rogue is rated for up to 29 mpg city and 36 mpg highway. Upgrading from front-wheel drive to all-wheel drive comes at a 1-mpg cost. The all-terrain tires on the Rogue Rock Creek also take a toll. That model boasts EPA estimates of 27 mpg city and 32 mpg highway.

On our 75-mph highway fuel-economy route, an all-wheel-drive Rogue Platinum with a 34-mpg EPA highway rating recorded a disappointing 31-mpg result. It also came in at 26 mpg combined (instead of the expected 31 mpg) during our compact SUV comparison test. For more information about the Rogue's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

Interior, Comfort, and Cargo

First Row: The Rogue’s cabin is fairly spacious. We appreciate the numerous useful cubbies up front, from the deep door pockets to the dashboard shelf to the center-console pass-through. Low-level models feature cloth seats, though leatherette and genuine leather are on the options list. The driver’s seat is comfortable, and top models look luxurious inside.

Second Row: Rear-seat legroom is accommodating for adults, as is headroom. Tall folks should have few complaints.

Cargo Capacity: Most Rogues offer 32 cubic feet of cargo space behind the rear seats, though the Platinum model has 37 cubes thanks to an extra underfloor compartment. With the back row folded, cargo capacity doubles to 74 cubic feet.

View Photos

Infotainment and Connectivity

  • Infotainment: 8.0-inch touchscreen (standard), 12.3-inch touchscreen (optional)
  • Connectivity: Bluetooth, wired Apple CarPlay and Android Auto compatibility (standard), wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto compatibility (optional)
  • Audio Systems: 4-speaker stereo (standard), 6-speaker stereo (optional), 10-speaker Bose stereo (optional)

All but the top two Rogue trims receive an 8.0-inch touchscreen infotainment system that supports smartphone-mirroring tech via a cable. SV models and above come with six speakers (two more than the base Rogue) as well as a Wi-Fi hotspot.

Nissan offers a 12.3-inch touchscreen, running Google software and enabling wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto functions, but shoppers will have to upgrade to the SL or Platinum trim to get it. We’d steer clear of that system for now. In a recent test of the Rogue, the 12.3-inch screen irked us with its slow responses and buried menus.

Safety and Driver-Assistance Features

Overall Safety Rating (NHTSA)

View Crash Test Results

The 2026 Rogue comes with a host of standard driver-assistance features to help it compete with rivals such as the Toyota RAV4 and the Subaru Forester. Nissan's ProPilot 2.1 system is also available on Platinum models and allows drivers to go hands-free on the highway.

  • Standard Safety Features: blind-spot monitoring, automated emergency braking, lane-departure warning
  • Optional Safety Features: adaptive cruise control with semi-autonomous driving mode, lane-centering assist, 360-degree camera system

For information about the Rogue’s crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

Warranty and Maintenance Coverage

Nissan's warranty coverage is unremarkable compared to rivals such as the Kia Sportage and the Hyundai Tucson. It does, however, provide up to three complimentary oil changes within the first two years or 24,000 miles.

  • Limited Warranty: three years or 36,000 miles
  • Powertrain Warranty: five years or 60,000 miles
  • Complimentary Maintenance: two years or 24,000 miles
